idiom_name: static methods on the class (static from/of) or module-level factory functions
implementation_notes: MDN documents static methods as the place for 'functions to create or clone' instances, so the class-level form is a static method plus a constructor that is made unreachable by a module token or by keeping the class unexported; module-level factory functions are the other common realization and avoid exporting the class at all. The runtime's own named constructors have the same shape - Array.from, Object.create, Promise.resolve, and Symbol.for, whose global registry makes repeated calls return the identical symbol - and Symbol.for is the honest model for the 'cache' motive, including its cost: registered symbols are never garbage collected.
pitfalls: JavaScript has no private constructors or private fields strong enough to stop `new Email(value)`: a module token or an unexported class is the only enforcement, otherwise the factory is a convention rather than a guarantee.
A static cache (Map/registry) lives for the module's lifetime and is shared mutable state - Symbol.for's registry is global and non-collectable, which is exactly the trade-off to accept on purpose.

Static methods are not bound: detaching one (const f = Email.from; f(x)) leaves `this` undefined, so a factory that refers to `this` breaks when passed as a callback - prefer module-level functions for callbacks.
